**Final search score: 93.8x the reference, using 8 of the 24 scorer calls.** The pick is in `final.py` and is exact on every check I ran.

| | search (scorer) | held-out (local seeds 101–103) |
|---|---|---|
| baseline | ~1.0 | 1 |
| first champion `c1_prefix` | 59.2 | 45 |
| final pick `final.py` (= `c13_small`) | **93.8** | 72 |

The scorer's timings moved by about 10% from run to run on this shared laptop. So 93.8 against `c9`'s 89.4 is within noise; the main gain over `c9` is that small awkward inputs no longer run slower than the reference.

**Why it's faster**
- **Identical records:** records with the same word set are grouped once and paired directly.
- **Short records:** for 5 to 8 distinct words, the 80% rule means the only possible match is the same set with one word removed. Those are found by direct lookup, with no index.
- **Records with 9 or more words:** these use a standard prefix-filtered join, which compares only records that share one of their rarest words. It also skips records of the wrong length and checks the exact rule `9·|A∩B| ≥ 4·(|A|+|B|)`.
- **Few long records:** if there are fewer than 40 sets of 8 or more words, it just compares them all, because building the index costs more than it saves. This was added after the awkward-input check: three records of about 20,000 words took 3× the reference time, right at the cut-off, and now take about the same as the reference.

**Other approaches tried**
- Integer bitsets with `bit_count`: 11× locally. Still compares every pair, so dropped.
- Counting word overlaps through an inverted index: 3× locally. Dropped.
- Extra filters on top of the prefix join:
  - a position-based filter: slower;
  - an index keyed by word and length: slower;
  - requiring two shared rare words (`c10`): better on small-vocabulary inputs, but scored 86.7.
- Ordering words alphabetically instead of by rarity: 13×. Common words then lead every record, so far too many records get compared.

**Checks**
- **Exactness:** every candidate matched the reference on about 270 small edge cases and on all timed inputs.
- **Harness vs scorer:** my harness ranked `c1 < c2 < c5` the same way the scorer did.
- **Awkward inputs** (`awkward.py`): all exact and none slower than the reference. They covered all-identical records (2 million pairs), all-empty records, a tiny vocabulary with big sets, huge records, Unicode whitespace, repeated words, and size-9 one-word swaps.

I stopped with 16 calls left. Two rounds of changes didn't beat the best official score, which is the skill's stop rule. The `c13` fix came after that, from the awkward-input step. One caution: the scorer's inputs seem to have fewer near-matches than mine, so it scored the short-record shortcut higher than my harness did.

Everything is in `dedup/`; the full candidate log is in `log.md`, and my harness is `harness.py`.
